content: [{"_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"There's a certain irony in the fact that the web started static, went dynamic, and is now swinging back toward static again. But the static sites of today aren't the hand-coded HTML pages of 1998. They're generated, optimized, and deployed to edge networks that serve them in milliseconds.","_key":"k1"}],"_key":"k0"},{"_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The pitch for server-rendered everything was compelling: dynamic content, personalization, real-time data. But most sites don't need most of that most of the time. A blog post doesn't need to be rendered on every request. A product page doesn't change every second.","_key":"k3"}],"_key":"k2"},{"_type":"block","style":"h2","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"The performance argument","_key":"k5"}],"_key":"k4"},{"_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"A static file served from a CDN is as fast as the web gets. No cold starts, no database queries, no server-side rendering overhead. The Time to First Byte is essentially the network latency to your nearest edge node. You can't beat physics.","_key":"k7"}],"_key":"k6"},{"_type":"block","style":"normal","children":[{"_type":"span","text":"And when you do need dynamic behavior, you can add it surgically. An island of interactivity in a sea of static HTML. The best of both worlds, without paying the cost of either at all times.","_key":"k9"}],"_key":"k8"}]
excerpt: Static sites aren't a step backwards. They're what you get when you take performance and simplicity seriously.
title: The Case for Static
